utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'd remind you, the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and we are finishing the questioning of Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When we broke off last, you had told us what you had been told about the burial of the bodies in Batajnica by one of your officers who had been stationed at Batajnica at the time. When you heard this, that is, when you discovered what was happening at your base or the base of one of your units, did you speak to Mr. Djordjevic about it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk to him about this directly because soon afterwards I returned to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you speak with him about it at any time thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In connection with this, I talked, and I think that this was immediately upon our return from the territory of Kosovo after the agreement was signed. But I wish to clarify this. When you asked me yesterday whether in the interviews you have had with ICTY investigators and at the special court in Belgrade, have you told the truth, or did you omit or suppress anything or leave anything out, specifically what was my suspicion about some of my statements had to do with this case because everything I told you yesterday about the activities of my units in Kosovo and Metohija as well as in other areas fully corresponds with what I stated, and I still stand by that. But there is something missing here, and it's something that I realised much later after having given those statements. So if you can give me the opportunity, maybe I could clarify that now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if it's relevant to the issues here. Can I just ask you, what you have to say is in respect to what topic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It mostly relates to the fact that I was convinced for a long time that within the perimeter of the centre of the SAJ Belgrade in Batajnica, only the bodies brought in from Kosovo and Metohija were buried. It was only much later that I learned that other bodies were also buried there. These were the bodies that were brought there later, bodies from the refrigerator trucks which appeared only later and from Petrovo Selo. And that actually all those bodies were brought to Batajnica and buried there, and that was the reason why something is missing in the statements I have given in connection with this during the last ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow you. You wish to tell us something about what you were told about the bodies that were buried at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wished to say that the information I had about the bodies buried in Batajnica related to the bodies brought from Kosovo and Metohija, and it was so for a long time. And I was not aware of the fact that actually the bodies that showed up sometime later, the bodies from refrigerator trucks from the Danube close to Bajina Basta also, and the bodies from Petrovo Selo, from the centre for the PJP training, that these bodies were also buried there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Trajkovic. We have heard evidence in this court from people who were involved in transporting and burying the bodies, so perhaps we could get to that aspect of your testimony later. But before I move away from this could I ask you: How did you become aware of the -- or how did you receive the information that bodies from Petrovo Selo and Bajina Basta were also buried at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was later that I realised and became aware that in addition to the bodies that had been brought from Kosovo on the first occasion, that a number of these bodies had been buried at Batajnica and that one part was thrown in the refrigerator truck into the Danube, some were thrown into the Perucac lake near Bajina Basta, and another part was buried in Petrovo Selo. So this is the information I had, that some of them were brought directly from Kosovo to Batajnica and that a certain number of other bodies were buried in these other three locations. But it was only later that I learned that after I had become aware of these refrigerator trucks that had appeared in the Danube and in the Perucac lake near Bajina Basta, that these bodies were also brought and buried in Batajnica. This is what I realised after I looked over the files, and then I realised the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which files are you referring to that informed you about these burials?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the statements I gave to ICTY investigators in my capacity as a suspect. At the time I became aware of the whole story because you can trust me that nothing was more difficult for me in my life. Even though I had been carrying out the kind of tasks that I had to do, nothing was more difficult for me than the awareness that the bodies that had been brought from Kosovo and Metohija were buried in one of my centres. It was very difficult for me to understand that something like this was possible. It was possible that something like that could have been done, but my first realisation was that these were the bodies or the mortal remains that had been brought directly from Kosovo. What I still am in dilemma about is whether this is done because I could never carry out any specific investigation, and it is not quite clear to me whether these are only the bodies that were brought from Kosovo or whether these were also the bodies that were discovered later in the refrigerator trucks and in other locations and were then brought from these locations to the centre in Batajnica and reburied there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. And that is what you wanted to clarify?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. I think we very much understand how difficult it would be for you or for anyone to hear that truck-loads of bodies were being brought to one's base or to territory that one controls for reburial. So when you were told this at the funeral by the man in charge of the base at Batajnica, I think you said you spoke to Mr. Djordjevic about it sometime after you returned from Kosovo, that is, after the withdrawal of the MUP and the VJ from Kosovo in June 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was more or less so because I think that I could not have talked to him about this through the communication that was normally used, and I noted yesterday that (redacted) told me that this was a state secret and that it was a very serious affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic, for the remainder of your testimony I'm going to ask you not to refer to (redacted) by name. There are reasons for that. He's a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I would respectfully ask the Court if what the witness just said and what I just said to him could be redacted from the public --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it will be enough if the name (redacted) is removed from -- redacted --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- as was done last evening in respect of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- the transcript yesterday afternoon late. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not wish to react yesterday because when we mention names we don't know -- that is to say the public does not know who is protected and who is not and what relates to what. But yesterday let me not name any names, but we mentioned the full first and last name of someone who is also a protected witness, so if this is being done, I think we should do the same for the other person as well, and I leave it up to the Chamber to consider this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many times did you speak to Mr. Djordjevic about what you had been told in respect to these truck-loads of bodies being taken to your base?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we talked about this two times. The first time was when I had a chance to ask him how come that this was done within the perimeter of our centre in Batajnica, and Mr. Djordjevic replied that this had been the decision of people who were much more important. He said something like, "This was the decision of people who are much more important than both you and me, and don't ask too many questions about this." And more or less I then realised what the head of our centre in Batajnica told me, that this was a state secret, but I also realised that the decision had been taken at a high level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall the approximate date or month of the first conversation?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime around the beginning of June 1999, and the next time was after we had retired from the territory of Kosovo and SAJ Pristina unit together with the SAJ Belgrade unit was accommodated at the centre in Batajnica. And then we had a conversation about whether it was possible to exhume those bodies and remove them to some other location. And then Mr. Djordjevic told me that I shouldn't be concerned about this and that the time would come for this to be done and that it would be done in one way or another; and that I shouldn't raise this issue anymore; and that when the time was right that I would be informed about how this would be done and what would be done with these bodies. And after that I did not raise the issue again. We were at the centre -- not myself personally, but the commands of both units were staying there. But as for the training, we didn't do any of the training that should have taken place in the part of the base where the bodies were buried until the exhumation became and until the forensic specialists and pathologists did their work. But this is something that is well-known to everyone by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Mr. Djordjevic indicate anything to you about the level of secrecy that was to be applied to this matter?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be frank, when I talked to Mr. Djordjevic I had the impression and I thought that these were mortal remains or bodies that had been directly brought from Kosovo and Metohija. However, I realised later on that my conversation with him and the answers I got from him related to the bodies that had been found in the two refrigerator trucks and in Petrovo Selo. Because I remember that on this occasion he told me that when decisions were taken what to do with this new discovery I asked him, "Chief, what was it that happened?" And he replied something like: "What can I tell you? All of my brave generals put their heads into this -- buried their heads into the sand and they left it to me to finish this part of the work." Now, whether this was a decision taken by the minister or in his office or if it had anything to do with a meeting that was held with President Milosevic with clearing up the terrain, I'm not certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, is that -- sorry, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was clear that the decision about this had been taken at a high level. That was highly probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was what I was just getting to. You told us that Mr. Djordjevic said the decision had been taken by more important people, and you took that to mean that at a -- the decision was taken at a higher level. Were you told, or did you receive any indication from Mr. Djordjevic as to who took the decision?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that the decision had been taken with regard to the sanitation and clearing up of the terrain. However, I do know that for this kind of purposes of clearing up the terrain General Ilic was in Kosovo in charge of this kind of operations. And we knew that he had been assigned a team leader of the team that was supposed to clear up the terrain in Kosovo battle-fields. I was under the impression that this meeting was also related to what Mr. Djordjevic told me during our conversation. I may have given a statement in which I quoted him by saying that this had been done at the meeting with Milosevic; however, later on I found out that this was the so-called task number two which involved the relocation of the mortal remains that was subsequently uncovered and their removal to Batajnica. Whether a meeting was -- about that was held with Mr. Milosevic or at the ministerial level, I'm not sure about that. But I am sure that on that occasion Mr. Djordjevic in response to my question about what was going on, he said, "What can I tell you? All my generals ran away and left their duty and left me to do this job." Only later did I realise that he was referring to the removal of the bodies that had been subsequently discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's -- if you don't mind, let's take this bit by bit. What I want you to focus on now is just what Mr. Djordjevic said, not what you might have heard or read later on that led you to conclusions. So let's limit ourselves to that for the time being. Did Mr. Djordjevic say anything in respect to any meetings where any relevant decisions were made?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did he say in respect to this meeting or more than one meeting, to these meetings, where that decision was made?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the decision had been taken at a much higher level than either of us were on, and that I shouldn't be concerned about that, particularly how the decision was taken. In a way, I felt that Mr. Djordjevic wanted to relieve me of this problem and to set my mind at peace until the whole situation is resolved and cleared. So basically what he said was that this decision was taken by people who were much more important than the two of us. This would be more or less the gist of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Mr. Djordjevic say anything about who participated in the making of the decision, who were these more important or higher-level persons who participated in the making of this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Djordjevic told me that people more important than either of us were involved, I didn't ask him their identity. I could only assume who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it from that you mean he did not say anything about the identity of these persons; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall about when the second conversation with Mr. Djordjevic occurred? That's the one at the base where the SAJ and the other unit were gathered.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second conversation did not take place at the base, but rather at the then-head office of the ministry. I said earlier that after the conflict in Kosovo and Metohija ended, these two units were accommodated and that the ministry was relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. I had the wrong place. But what I'm just interested in is approximately when. If you can't recall the date, the month and the year would do.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You referred to Mr. Ilic. Can you just remind us what was Mr. Ilic's position in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time General Ilic held the position of the head of the criminal police investigation administration in the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the conflict, March to June 1999, did you see him in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least once. I saw him at least once and perhaps twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where did you see him, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in Pristina, that's for sure. He was in this provisional staff of MUP for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say he was in the provisional staff, you mean he was -- well, what do you mean? Was he located where the staff was set up?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's where the staff was at the time because the building where the Kosovo and Metohija staff was located all had been bombed, and they had to move around quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you speak with him?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just greeted each other, as is the usual practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From your contact with other senior MUP personnel active in Kosovo at the time, were you able to ascertain or receive information as to what was his role in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In conversation with my colleagues, I gathered that he was charged with the sanitation and hygiene measures or clearing up in Kosovo and Metohija and that that's why he was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said "that's why he was stationed there." Were you able to ascertain from your colleagues how often and for what periods of time he would spend in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I'm not sure whether he was stationed there or to some other nearby location. I can only say that I met him at least once. And believe me, I never thought about how long he would be staying there in order to participate in certain operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Knowing what you know now in respect to the movement of the bodies and the burial of the bodies, that is, the movement of the bodies from Kosovo and the burial at Batajnica, in your assessment could this operation have taken place without the knowledge of the membership of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, that is to say I don't think it could have happened without their knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we go into private session just for two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did what that person said - and let's not call the name of the person - reflect your attitude in screening persons or screening out persons who had been members of paramilitary units, including those or especially those that were active in Croatia, and ensuring that they were never part of your unit? Was that your attitude at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm afraid I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very good. I'll rephrase it. Did the evidence of that person, former member of the SAJ that I just read to you, reflect your attitude in respect to paramilitary persons or persons who were members of paramilitary units joining the SAJ, that you were opposed to it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but this person is not an ex-member. He's still discharging the same duties that he did back then. Therefore, I'm not quite sure that I can answer this question by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I don't want you to say yes or no. I want you to tell us whether or not what he said correctly reflects your attitude in respect to paramilitary members joining the SAJ. He said you told him that if he had been a member of any paramilitary unit, including any paramilitary unit that is active in Croatia, you would not tolerate it and you did not want anybody like that in your unit. Does that correctly reflect your attitude in respect to incorporating paramilitaries into the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the person involved was a member of regular MUP forces in Croatia before he joined us. I honestly never took part in any such interviews with him because with regard to the job that he was doing in Batajnica at the time, he was a simple labourer who were supposed to do a certain job. Whether he mixed me with someone else, probably his own commander, Mr. Simovic or not, I'm not sure. But I definitely never had any such interview about these circumstances with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have a policy in respect to the incorporation of former members of paramilitaries into the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances the conditions set -- laid down for membership in the units that I commanded were fully clear; however, in the situation that our country found itself in from the 24th of March until the end of the NATO aggression against our country had changed the entire picture all together with respect to the things that you're asking me about. So maybe we can elaborate on that a little. However, in regular times I can give you precisely which conditions have to be met by applicants who wish to join the units that I was in command of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I will not pursue that issue any further for the sake of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, may it please you, that is the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would appreciate a break so that I can consolidate my notes, and hopefully I will be brief and expeditious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They're lovely words. Let us hope we find them well proved. If it will help, we'll have the first break now, Mr. Djurdjic, rather than at the normal time, and we will resume at 20 minutes to 4.00. -- Recess taken at 3.07 p.m. -- On resuming at 3.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Trajkovic. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, member of the Defence team of the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic. Here with me today is Ms. Marie O'Leary and Mr. Aleksandar Popovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I have only a couple of questions in order to clarify some of the answers that you have given today. Earlier today you mentioned a meeting with Mr. Milosevic. Were you by chance present at this meeting with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Have you ever attended any meeting with President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with him but not in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you come about the information that this meeting in Milosevic's office took place, the one that you mentioned today?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this meeting with Mr. Milosevic from a gentleman who appeared here as a protected witness, therefore I'm not sure whether I should mention his name or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Don't say anything before we move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether during the war in all of Serbia, including Kosovo and Metohija, there were on-site investigations carried out in all incidents where death was the result whenever such incidents were known?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly so in Serbia. Whether this was carried out in Kosovo, all these on-site investigations, I cannot say with any certainty, especially not for the year 1999. But I believe that if the conditions were met to do that, that it was done in Kosovo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And while you were there in Kosovo, did you know that representatives of the branch offices of the SUP did that, that they went out onto the scene whenever death occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, whenever it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know and did you sign any note about the conversation with the witness that -- whom we mentioned a minute ago and whose name you don't have to mention now?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was rather a private conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would ask to see Exhibit MFI D48. And while we're waiting for the document to appear on the screen, Your Honours, as it has been translated I would ask for it to be admitted into evidence after we have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic, can you see your name anywhere here on this first page?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot see my name on the second page either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just let me say it's D004-2898 -- correction: 2892, this was the document. And the document that should help us with the identification, and now I wish to propose that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told it's not yet been uploaded into the electronic system. It may have been translated, but the procedure has not been followed. This is MFI D48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We now have the number 2892 of the translation, so we can receive as Exhibit D48 the earlier one that was marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic, you noted a little while ago that you had this conversation with Mr. Djordjevic when you asked him how come that all these bodies ended up at the centre in Batajnica. Am I right that he told you that it was decided at a level much higher than you and him that the bodies be buried there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right that you during the war and until 2001 did not have any knowledge about the transportation of bodies from Kosovo and Metohija into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first learned about the bodies buried at the centre in Batajnica somewhere around April 1999, and I understood that these were bodies brought to Batajnica from Kosovo. So it was not before 2001, but it was in April 1999. That was when I learned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And tell me, did you hear this from (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from (redacted) that a great number of bodies had been brought there, and of course, I connected that with the clearing of the terrain in Kosovo. And when he said these were great numbers, I suppose that they couldn't be from any other location or any other area, but that these were the mortal remains of people from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was your conclusion; right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is need I think for another redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've just been discussing that. It's simply said in evidence, but as attention has now been drawn to it I think we better redact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic, am I right that your opinion that without the knowledge of the Joint Command the bodies could not have been transported from Kosovo and Metohija into Serbia is only your assumption?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I did not attend the meetings at which this was decided, it's absolutely just my assumption that this was done on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija -- that nothing could be done on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija without the knowledge of the staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Trajkovic, what was Mr. Djordjevic's attitude when he told you about the burial of these bodies in Batajnica? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVKO TRAJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have more or less replied to that, that we did not discuss this at any length. When I asked him why this had been done in Batajnica and how come that they had been buried there, he replied more or less that I shouldn't be concerned about that, that the decision had been taken at a much higher level, and that now I shouldn't be bothered about this too much but that I should focus on the problems relating to my own units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I have no re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Trajkovic, you'll be pleased to learn that that concludes the questions that will be asked of you. The Chamber has listened with interest to your evidence, and we would like to thank you for your attendance here and the assistance that you have been able to give. You may of course now return to your normal activities and a court officer will assist you from the courtroom. So thank you indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is the extent of the witnesses we have available for this week. We have one scheduled for next Monday, pending -- well, we expect to have that witness on Monday, but that depends on -- some degree on the health status of that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you are not yet in a position to know about the attendance of that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Our arrangement was that we would speak with him on -- today or tomorrow - I think it's tomorrow - but we are scheduled to speak with him tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears to the Chamber important that the witness attend next week or the following Monday if we are to finish the evidence this month for the Prosecution. So we would encourage you to do all that is possible to ensure that that occurs. Now, you have mentioned two other witnesses, one of whom is to be heard commencing Monday, the 26th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there anything known more of the third witness at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We are pulling out all the stops, so to speak, to locate that witness. But as I indicated before, we would not seek any additional time for that witness if that witness is not available by that last week of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment then we will -- sorry, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have something to ask for, and I have a proposition. The Prosecution case is almost finished. We are working very intensively on preparing the Defence case, so I would ask you, if possible, as we shall anyway be working in the week of the 26th October, that if we can have the same -- the next witness in the same week because in the meantime we could be preparing the Defence case. I think this would be efficient and useful, and I think that we would finish both of these witnesses during this week when the Chamber planned to have the completion of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The obvious difficulty with that proposition concerns the health of the next witness. Whenever that witness is able to be here, I think we need to ensure that the witness is heard so that we don't find that in two or three weeks' time the witness is again not well enough to attend. I know that will be of inconvenience potentially to you and those preparing the case in Belgrade, but it's going to be I think more important that we ensure that we hear the evidence of that witness whenever he can be here to give it. Now, it may mean that we will have to delay a day or so to enable you to travel to be here, but I think it would be putting at risk the completion of the Prosecution case if we simply adjourned now until the week of the 26th of October. Of course, we might find we've missed the one opportunity of hearing that witness. I'm sorry about that, Mr. Djurdjic. We normally do what we can to accommodate you, but that appears to be a significant issue. So what we must do is adjourn now until next Monday. It is possible that in the meantime we will learn that the witness cannot be here, in which event of course we will advise you or the -- the Prosecution will advise you so that you don't have to travel. Or if you're still here, you then are free then to return to Belgrade and make arrangements to be there for the next fortnight. Of course it will be important that you be concentrating in this time on the preparation of the Defence case, as you say that you are. But I hope you realise that for the reason indicated we really need to seize the opportunity, if it's available, of hearing the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My hope was just that the witness's health would be better and better, so in that sense I had this proposal. But I absolutely accept any of your considerations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will proceed on that basis, and we expect to hear from you, Mr. Stamp, the moment it is known whether or not the witness will be here next Monday. And if it is that some other date is a date that the witness can be here, it may be that we will have to change the hearing date from next Monday to that other date to fit in with the health of the witness. But the Chamber's preference is to hear the witness as soon as he is available so that we do not miss the opportunity all together of hearing him. And beyond that, we have what will be the last witness for the Prosecution on Monday, the 26th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you. Well, we adjourn now, with a view to resuming on Monday next. -- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.07 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 5th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
